The central question is: when a RAG system retrieves and concatenates multiple passages into a long context, does the KV cache eviction policy interact with the structure of query-document relevance in ways that degrade answer quality beyond what perplexity or cache hit rate metrics would reveal? KV caches in long-context transformers are expensive, so systems like H2O, SnapKV, or sliding-window attention selectively evict tokens based on accumulated attention scores or recency — but those heuristics were benchmarked on narrative or conversational text, not on the bursty, non-uniform attention patterns that RAG produces, where a 200-token passage buried at position 3,000 may be the only thing the model needs to answer the query. The key concepts are: eviction policies (which tokens get dropped and when), query locality (whether relevant tokens cluster together or are scattered across the context), and the "lost in the middle" failure mode, which shows that even without eviction, retrieval position alone degrades recall — eviction compounds this asymmetrically. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is that attention-score-based eviction creates a self-reinforcing bias: tokens that weren't attended to in early layers get evicted before later layers can use them for multi-hop reasoning, and since RAG relevance is often sparse and late-activating, the eviction policy can silently amputate exactly the evidence the model needs, with no decoding error signal — the model still produces fluent, confident output, just grounded in the wrong passages.

H2O (Zhang et al., 2023) maintains a fixed-size KV cache budget by scoring each token with a running sum of attention weights it has received across all heads in the current layer, then greedily evicting the lowest-scoring tokens before processing the next layer — critically, this decision is made layer-by-layer, so a token evicted at layer 8 never participates in the residual stream at layer 16, even if layer-16 attention heads would have retrieved it heavily. SnapKV (Li et al., 2024) is slightly more sophisticated: it pools attention patterns from the last few "observation" tokens in the prompt (typically the final 16–32 tokens before generation begins) across all heads to decide which KV pairs to compress away, which means eviction is determined by what the query end of the prompt attends to in a single forward pass — not by what will matter during multi-token generation. The structural disadvantage for deep-layer relevance emerges from a well-documented property of transformer circuits: early layers perform syntactic and surface-level matching (lexical overlap, entity co-occurrence), while deeper layers — especially layers in the latter two-thirds of large models like LLaMA-2-70B or Mistral — handle semantic inference, coreference across long gaps, and multi-hop composition. A RAG passage that is relevant because of an inferential relationship to the query (e.g., "the compound inhibits enzyme X" is relevant to "what treats disease Y that enzyme X causes") may receive near-zero early-layer attention since there is little surface overlap, and H2O will evict it before the layers capable of recognizing the inferential link ever process it. Empirically, this is consistent with findings in the Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluations and the RULER benchmark (Hsieh et al., 2024), where performance degrades sharply when the relevant "needle" lacks lexical similarity to the query — exactly the condition that defeats attention-score-based eviction signals. The deeper problem is that neither H2O nor SnapKV has access to a globally consistent relevance signal: each makes a local, greedy decision with partial information, and the eviction is irreversible once the forward pass moves on.

The core architectural constraint is that the KV cache stores activations at each layer independently and in sequence: to defer eviction to layer 24, you must have already materialized and stored the full KV tensors for layers 1–23 for every token, which means peak memory scales as O(L × S × d) where L is the number of layers deferred over, S is the sequence length, and d is the head dimension — precisely the memory pressure that eviction was introduced to relieve in the first place, creating a circular dependency. In a 70B-parameter model with 80 layers and a 32K-token context, storing full KV tensors across even half the layers before making any eviction decision would require tens of gigabytes of additional activation memory per request, which is why production systems like vLLM and TensorRT-LLM make eviction decisions greedily per-layer and discard the tensors immediately. One partial sidestep is lazy eviction with lightweight scoring proxies: instead of storing full KV tensors, you store a compressed representation (e.g., a single accumulated attention-weight scalar per token per layer) across layers and only commit to eviction after aggregating scores from layers 1–N, which is what PyramidKV (Cai et al., 2024) approximates by allocating different cache budgets per layer based on observed attention entropy, implicitly giving deeper layers more retention capacity without full deferral. A more direct sidestep is speculative KV retention: Griffin (De et al., 2024) and related recurrent-hybrid architectures sidestep the problem structurally by using linear recurrence for most layers and full attention only in selected layers, so the "deep layer decides" problem is reframed — only a few layers maintain a KV cache at all, and those layers are chosen to be the ones with globally compositional attention patterns. The most direct attack on the deferral problem in pure-transformer systems is cross-layer KV sharing with deferred eviction gates, explored in work like MagicPIG (Chen et al., 2024), which uses locality-sensitive hashing to predict which tokens will be attended to in future layers based on query vectors, effectively acting as a learned proxy for deep-layer relevance without materializing the full tensors. The common thread in all these approaches is that they replace the "wait and see" strategy with a prediction of deep-layer relevance using cheaper signals — which reframes the problem from a memory-management question into a learned retrieval question, and inherits all the generalization risks that come with that.

The distributional mismatch has two concrete layers: first, pretraining corpora (C4, The Pile, FineWeb) consist overwhelmingly of contiguous natural text where local coherence means that surface attention patterns are reliable proxies for semantic importance — the sentence after a topic sentence is almost always relevant, so early-layer attention scores trained on that data learn to reward syntactic proximity and lexical overlap, neither of which holds in RAG contexts where relevant passages are non-contiguous, heterogeneous in style, and separated by semantically unrelated chunks. Second, the attention patterns that eviction predictors implicitly learn during pretraining reflect a generative objective — predict the next token given all prior tokens — which biases retained context toward tokens that reduce perplexity of the continuation, whereas RAG inference requires retaining tokens that answer a query that appears at the end of the context, a retrieval objective that is structurally absent from standard causal LM pretraining and only partially addressed by instruction fine-tuning. Concretely, LSH-based predictors like MagicPIG hash query and key vectors into buckets calibrated on pretraining-like attention distributions; when your RAG corpus contains domain-specific technical text (e.g., clinical notes, patent claims, legal contracts), the key vectors for relevant passages may systematically fall outside the high-probability hash buckets, producing collision patterns that look like low relevance to the predictor even when deep-layer attention would be high. To measure whether this mismatch is causing eviction errors on your corpus, the right instrument is a counterfactual eviction audit: run your RAG pipeline twice — once with the eviction policy active and once with full KV cache retention (feasible on a sample at evaluation time) — and diff the model's output logit distributions over the answer span, flagging cases where eviction caused a rank reversal in the probability of the correct answer token; this is more diagnostic than end-to-end accuracy because it isolates eviction-caused errors from retrieval errors and prompt sensitivity. You can further localize which evicted tokens caused the degradation by a token-level ablation: replay the forward pass with each evicted token's KV pair restored one at a time and measure the resulting logit change for the answer, which gives you an empirical relevance signal you can correlate against the predictor's score to directly quantify the mismatch magnitude on your specific corpus. If the correlation between predictor score and counterfactual logit impact is low (e.g., Spearman ρ < 0.3), you have quantitative evidence that the eviction policy is operating near-randomly with respect to actual answer relevance, and you can segment by passage type, query type, or retrieval rank to identify which subpopulations drive the failure.

The most tractable intervention is passage-type-aware cache pinning: use a lightweight classifier (a fine-tuned BERT-scale model, or even a regex/heuristic over passage structure) to tag retrieved passages as inferential/multi-hop at retrieval time, then mark those passages' KV entries as eviction-ineligible — effectively reserving a protected partition of the cache budget for them, analogous to how OS page tables implement "wired" memory pages that the eviction daemon cannot touch. This requires no base model changes, integrates at the cache management layer (e.g., as a custom eviction policy in vLLM's block manager), and directly targets the confirmed failure mode without disturbing eviction behavior for passages where the default policy works. The immediate new failure mode is budget starvation: if your retrieval pipeline returns many passages that the classifier tags as inferential — which is likely in multi-hop QA datasets like MuSiQue or 2WikiMultiHopQA where most retrieved passages have inferential structure — the protected partition consumes the majority of the cache budget, leaving insufficient space for the remaining passages and degrading performance on queries that require breadth of coverage rather than depth of reasoning. A subtler second failure mode is classifier-eviction mismatch under distribution shift: the passage-type classifier is trained on a fixed typology, but real RAG corpora contain passages that are inferential in context but not in isolation (a passage that looks like a simple factual claim becomes inferential only when combined with the specific query), so the classifier will miss context-dependent inferential passages and over-protect context-independent ones, reintroducing systematic eviction errors for a different subpopulation. There is also a position interaction effect: pinned passages accumulate KV entries that persist across the entire generation, which means their attention scores continue to influence all subsequent layers and heads — if the pinned passages are not actually relevant to a given query (false positives from the classifier), they act as persistent attention sinks that pull probability mass away from correct answer tokens, a mechanism similar to the "distractor passage" effect documented in Shi et al. (2023), where irrelevant but salient context degrades answer accuracy by 30%+ on GSM8K-style reasoning.

The property a better pinning signal needs to capture is query-conditioned inferential load: specifically, how many reasoning steps must be composed between the query and this passage before the passage contributes to the answer, which is a joint property of the query-passage pair and cannot be read off either in isolation — a passage stating "compound X inhibits kinase Y" is a direct lookup for the query "what does compound X do?" but is a second-hop inferential node for "what treats disease Z?" where the link runs through kinase Y. The ideal signal is therefore something like the expected attention depth at which the passage first receives high attention weight given this specific query, which is exactly what the counterfactual audit measures but at unacceptable latency for cache management (it requires a full forward pass). The closest existing approximation is cross-encoder reranking scores: models like Cohere Rerank, BGE-Reranker-v2, or monoT5 compute a query-passage relevance score via full cross-attention between query and passage tokens, and critically, the internal representations they build to produce that score capture some of the inferential distance — a passage with low cross-encoder score despite high bi-encoder score is a signal that the relevance is not surface-level, which correlates with the inferential structure that defeats eviction policies. The operational problem is latency: cross-encoder reranking at cache-management latency (sub-5ms per passage) is feasible only for short passages with a distilled model (e.g., a 6-layer cross-encoder like those in the BEIR benchmark evaluation suite runs ~2ms per passage on GPU), but the score you get is a scalar relevance estimate, not a decomposed measure of inferential depth, so you are still using a proxy rather than the true signal. A more targeted approximation is the score gap between bi-encoder and cross-encoder rankings: passages that rank highly on bi-encoder (BM25 or dense retrieval) but receive a large upward revision from the cross-encoder are ones where surface similarity underestimates true query-relevance — this gap is computable from retrieval artifacts already present in most RAG pipelines, adds no new inference cost, and directly flags passages where early-layer attention (which behaves like a bi-encoder) will undervalue what deep-layer attention (which behaves like a cross-encoder) would find important. This bi-encoder/cross-encoder score gap is not a perfect inferential depth measure, but it is causally aligned with the eviction failure mechanism: it identifies exactly the passages where the shallow signal used by H2O or SnapKV diverges from the deep signal that actually determines answer quality, making it the most principled cheap proxy currently available without architectural changes.

When the retrieved set grows beyond roughly 50–100 passages, full cross-encoder reranking becomes the dominant latency term: a 6-layer cross-encoder running at ~2ms per passage on a single A100 takes 100–200ms just for reranking at k=100, which exceeds the entire LLM prefill budget for short-context queries and makes the reranker the system bottleneck rather than the cache — at that point you have traded an eviction quality problem for a latency problem without net gain. The first thing that breaks architecturally is the rerank-then-truncate assumption: most RAG pipelines retrieve k=100, rerank, take top-k=5, then pass to the LLM, which means the cross-encoder only ever scores the top retrieved passages, but eviction-robust caching needs the score gap for all passages that will actually enter the context window, and if you are doing long-context RAG with k=20–50 passages in context, you need reranking scores for all of them, not just the top 5. The pressure this creates pushes toward late-interaction models like ColBERT-v2 (Santhanam et al., 2022), which precompute per-token embeddings at index time and compute query-passage interaction scores via MaxSim at retrieval time — ColBERT achieves cross-encoder-quality ranking at bi-encoder latency (~4ms for k=1000 on GPU with PLAID indexing), and its per-token interaction scores are structurally richer than a bi-encoder dot product, providing a cheaper approximation of the inferential depth signal without full cross-encoder inference. A second architectural shift is cascaded retrieval with adaptive reranking depth: retrieve a large candidate set with a bi-encoder, apply the cross-encoder only to the passages that will actually enter the LLM context (not the full candidate set), and use the bi-encoder score alone as a pre-filter to reduce the reranking surface — this is what Contextual Retrieval (Anthropic, 2024) and RAGatouille approximate, keeping reranking cost proportional to context window size rather than retrieval candidate set size. The deeper implication for system architecture is that eviction-robust caching and low-latency retrieval pull in opposite directions on the reranking budget: eviction robustness wants rich query-passage interaction signals for everything in context, while latency wants to minimize cross-encoder calls, and the resolution is to treat the LLM prefill itself as a reranking signal — specifically, the attention weights from the first few transformer layers during prefill are computable anyway and can be used to trigger post-hoc pinning decisions mid-prefill, converting the latency problem into an online decision problem that amortizes the scoring cost across the prefill computation already being performed.
